articles.title: Apple’s Folding iPhone Debuts Alongside 5 Other Launches
articles.summary: Apple just unveiled its first folding iPhone alongside five other major product launches. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new.
articles.body: Today, Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, announced a handful of new iPhones, Apple Watches and AirPods. It was Ternus’ first big announcement since taking over for Tim Cook earlier this month. The most newsworthy addition to the lineup? A long-rumored foldable phone (more on that below). Below is everything you need to know about these new launches — including pre-order and in-store dates. New iPhones Apple announced three new iPhones: the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone Pro Max and the all-new foldable iPhone Duo. Notably absent was a standard iPhone 18 — Apple may be holding that model, along with a new iPhone 18e, until spring 2027. The Pro lineup keeps a familiar look but gains Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, built on a 2-nanometer process, along with a variable-aperture 48-megapixel main camera for better low-light and depth control. This phone is $100 more expensive than last year’s model, starting at $1,199. Apple also announced the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which starts at $1,299. The major difference between the two is screen size and battery life. The Pro has a 6.3-inch screen compared to the Max’s 6.9-inch screen. As for battery, the Pro offers up to 24 hours, while the Max offers up to 30 hours. Pre-orders for these phones open Saturday, September 12, with devices in stores September 18. This is the big one: Apple’s first-ever foldable iPhone. It opens like a book into a roughly 7.8-inch interior display, with a smaller exterior screen for everyday use when it’s closed. Closed, it’s about the size of a passport. Apple built the Duo around its new in-house C2 modem — the company’s second-generation cellular chip, which Apple says is 50 percent faster than its predecessor while using 15 percent less power. The dual rear camera system can be used on both sides of the fold at once, so you can show someone what you’re seeing on a FaceTime call. Apple also packed in two separate battery cells, rating the Duo for up to 44 hours of use on the outer display alone, or about 24 hours using both screens. The iPhone Duo will launch with two color options — white and dark blue. Pricing will start at $1,999 for 256GB of storage and the release is on a later schedule than the rest of the lineup: pre-orders begin October 16, with the device arriving in stores October 23. Apple Watch Apple also refreshed its smartwatch lineup with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 — and, in a bit of good news, neither watch got a price increase. Both watches are available for pre-order now. The Apple Watch Series 12 centers on a redesigned Health Sensing System, paired with the new S11 chip. Its optical and electrical sensors have been rebuilt with larger, more power-efficient green LEDs, enabling far more frequent monitoring — the watch takes background heart rate readings every five seconds and measures heart rate variability as often as every five minutes, which Apple says is 60 times more frequent than on the Series 11. That data feeds a new Readiness score, calculated each morning from recent activity, vitals, and sleep, giving wearers a single number to gauge how much they can take on that day. It’s available in eight finishes, including two ceramic options in Pearl White and Night Blue, and the aluminum models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass. Beyond health tracking, the Series 12 adds AI-driven software features tied to the new Siri, including a Live Rewind function that lets you replay the last 15 seconds of audio you just missed, and Siri Recap, which generates summaries of conversations picked up by the watch’s microphone. It retains the familiar 42mm and 46mm case sizes and standard safety features like Fall Detection and Emergency SOS, and is rated WR50 and IP6X for water and dust resistance. It starts at $399, the same price as the Series 11, and is available for pre-order now ahead of a September 18 release. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is built around the same S11 chip and redesigned Health Sensing System as the Series 12, but tuned for endurance athletes and outdoor use. Battery life gets a major boost too: Apple rates it for up to 50 hours of everyday use, up to 18 hours of standard workout tracking with full GPS and heart rate monitoring, and up to 45 hours in a new Max Extended Workout mode — enough to cover a 100-mile race. It’s available in two titanium finishes, natural and black, and retains the built-in satellite communications that let wearers stay connected off the grid. Like the Series 12, the Ultra 4 also picks up Siri AI and Audio Intelligence features powered by the S11 chip, plus the ability to start a request on iPhone and pick it up seamlessly on the watch. It keeps the rugged design and precision dual-frequency GPS that have defined the Ultra line. Pricing holds steady at $799, the same as the Ultra 3, with pre-orders open now for the September 18 release. AirPods Apple unveiled the AirPods 5, its next mainstream earbuds, priced at $129, or $149 for the version with a wireless charging case. The AirPods 5 deliver up to 1.5x more active noise cancellation than the previous generation and are powered by a new H2 chip. They also have dynamic head tracking, adaptive audio to switch between noise cancelling and transparency mode, depending on your environment. Similar to other AirPod models, they also have IP57 rating for dust, sweat, and water resistance. On the software side, they offer hands-free access to the new Siri AI and real-time Live Translation. Battery life is up to 4 hours with ANC on the base model, or 5 hours (22 total with the case) on the version with a USB-C Wireless Charging Case, which also supports Qi and Apple Watch charging. AirPods 5 are available for pre-order now, shipping September 18. Are there any new Macs or iPads? Nothing new was announced on that front today — this event was focused on iPhone, Watch and AirPods. Apple already refreshed the Mac mini and Mac Studio with M6 and M5 Ultra chips last month, and any further Mac or iPad updates will likely come at a separate event later this year or even next spring. Why did some prices go up? Apple didn’t detail its reasoning beyond pointing to component costs, but the iPhone 18 Pro price increase tracks with a broader trend this year: rising memory and storage prices have pushed up costs across phones, laptops and other electronics throughout 2026. I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness, beauty, home and lifestyle. I have written about the “no-touch” phone law, the best screen protectors and more. For this story, I researched all of Apple’s new offerings and watched their announcement event. articles.title: Thailand wants more from its data center boom due to its huge demand
articles.summary: Thailand puts 166 data center projects on hold after officials discover major gaps in power, water, and site planning
articles.body:
Thailand has frozen 166 data center projects to develop new rules covering electricity, water, locations, safety, and economic returns.

Officials found limited information on the country's total data center activity, with only 35 operating centers and 11 receiving investment support through Thailand's Board of Investment.

The government is reviewing existing sites and planning new rules to address concerns about electricity demand, water use, site selection, construction safety, environmental effects, and resource costs associated with large data centers.

Thailand has frozen 166 data center projects pending new national rules

Officials found major gaps in data on existing data centers

Large data centers are putting new pressure on water supplies

Thailand has halted 166 data center projects while officials work on new rules for electricity, water, locations, safety, and economic returns.

The pause covers 49 facilities already being built and another 117 projects still waiting for approval from government agencies.

Officials say the review aims to keep attracting investment while ensuring data centers provide jobs, technology gains, and useful services for Thailand.

Thailand puts data center growth under review

The decision followed a recent meeting of the national data center policy board, which ordered four groups to draft standards within one month.

Four subcommittees will each examine a different area: economic benefits, infrastructure needs, site and location standards, and environmental protection.

The review comes after agencies found limited information about the country's total data center activity, including facilities already running and projects awaiting approval.

Information from 16 government bodies showed that 35 data centers were operating, with 11 receiving investment support through Thailand's Board of Investment.

Another 24 facilities gained approval through other routes, while several smaller centers were operated by financial institutions.

The government now wants one central system showing project locations, approval status, electricity sources, water supplies, planning rules, and other key details.

That system would allow agencies to examine the combined effects of multiple facilities instead of reviewing each project through separate approval channels.

Bangkok has also begun checking existing sites, with six projects seeking approval and each requiring between 9 MW and 23 MW of power.

Three received approval and began operations from 2022 through 2024, while the remaining applications will stay frozen until national standards are ready.

Water, power, and economic gains shape new rules

The planned rules will cover electricity demand, water use, site selection, construction safety, backup fuel storage, environmental effects, and distance from nearby buildings.

Officials are also reviewing whether facilities using more than 2 MW should face rules similar to those applied to industrial businesses.

Large centers need constant power and significant water for cooling, creating concerns about pressure on local networks and supplies.

The government also wants prices for water and electricity to account for direct and indirect costs linked to large facilities.

That approach is intended to prevent households and other businesses from carrying costs tied to data center resource use.

Future projects could face a competitive approval process that weighs employment, technology transfer, clean energy use, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said data centers matter to Thailand's economy, although the government lacked complete information about existing facilities and planned developments.

The government is now seeking full details on data centers so it can develop laws that will guide future investment decisions.

Rather than expanding server capacity without assessing their demand, Thailand wants to gain more value from incoming projects.

The pause does not signal an end to Thailand's data center ambitions, since officials continue seeking investment while examining how growth should proceed.

articles.title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
articles.summary: Declassified documents show Spanish and Moroccan authorities were alerted to social media calls for a mass migrant crossing the day before tens of thousands entered Ceuta.
articles.body:
Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.

The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.

On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.

Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants .

In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".

The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades."

It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.

The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.

Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.

However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.

Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".

But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim.

"They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.

Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".

The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available.

Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have forseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".

A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".

Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing.

"The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

articles.title: German-Swiss border crossing reopens after explosives alert
articles.summary: A border crossing between Germany and Switzerland reopened late on Wednesday after shutting for several hours due to an explosives alert. During a border che...
articles.body:
Border crossing between Germany and Switzerland at Rheinfelden reopens after explosives alert and vehicle inspection triggers evacuation and closure.

Explosives detection dogs reacted to a car with German number plates, leading to evacuation of designated danger zone and closure of A861 highway.

Two German nationals taken into custody following suspected security threat, but police confirm no hazardous substances found and motorway reopened.

A border crossing between Germany and Switzerland reopened late on Wednesday after shutting for several hours due to an explosives alert.

During a border check in the afternoon at the Rheinfelden crossing, explosives detection dogs reacted to a car with German number plates.

A designated danger zone was evacuated due to the suspected security threat, and special units from the Federal Police were called in.

The two occupants of the car, both German nationals, were taken into custody. By the evening, it was unclear whether they remained in custody.

The police did not confirm media reports suggesting that the men were father and son and that both had been the subject of a manhunt.

"No hazardous substances were found," said a police spokesman. "The motorway has been reopened."

The closure affected the A861. The motorway links the A98 on the German side with the Swiss A3, and is used by around 30,000 vehicles each day.

According to the German automobile club ADAC, there were traffic jams stretching for several kilometres on both sides.

images.caption: A police officer stands on the A861 highway near Rheinfelden, with the border crossing into Switzerland visible in the background. Following a suspected discovery of explosives during a vehicle inspection, the border crossing into Switzerland at the Rheinfelden-Autobahn checkpoint has been closed in both directions. articles.title: Are wealthy buyers stoking St Andrews' housing crisis?
articles.summary: New figures shows nearly one in five properties in St Andrews were registered to an address outside of Scotland when purchased.
articles.body:
A world class university and the home of golf in a pretty coastal town underline the appeal to many of living in St Andrews.

But the Fife town is in the grips of an affordable housing crisis, where property prices are being stoked by the influence of wealthy buyers from outwith Scotland.

New data shows nearly one in five properties in St Andrews were registered to an address outside of Scotland when purchased, including 164 buyers from the United States alone.

Locals say more needs to be done to improve the balance between serving the town's much-valued students and tourists, and its permanent residents.

The last census put the population of St Andrews at just over 16,000.

But on its busiest days, walking through the town can feel more like navigating the centre of a busy European city.

For locals, the economic benefits of the town's appeal to visitors are clear but the knock-on effect for house and rental prices is taking its toll.

Fife Council has said finding reasonably priced housing in St Andrews is a "major challenge" and has put in measures such as quotas of affordable housing in new developments to try and help.

And the town's university has capped its student numbers at around 10,000 for nearly a decade now because of the pressure on housing and other local amenities.

Francesca Bisi, a fourth year PhD student in the School of Art History, knows all about these pressures as she is commuting to her studies from a nearby village after being unable to get affordable accommodation in the Fife town.

"It has been really stressful to try to navigate the housing market here, and even in my fourth year it's something that is still causing a huge challenge," she said.

''It distracts from my work, distracts from my studies and really takes a huge toll on my mental health as well.

"I know that any savings that I've been able to put aside that year always end up being drained in whatever down payment because in this market you know you can't really afford to be picky with what you find and you just feel lucky that you found any place at all.''

Average advertised rents in St Andrews over the last year have been £1,702 per month, compared with the Scottish average of £1,245 per month, according to data from property firm Rightmove.

Amy Elvins, of the St Andrews University Students' Association, said this has caused a disparity in a housing market dogged by a lack of supply.

She said: "The high rents in St Andrews have ultimately meant that all power lies with landlords, which means that students are potentially having to work full time.

"It has created a market in which the understanding is that all houses in town will be filled so it doesn't really matter the standard and the price that they are.

"It means that members of the community are also being priced out and what we ultimately need is more affordable rentable housing."

Where are property buyers in St Andrews from?

The vast majority of property and land in Scotland is registered to people and companies based in the country.

But Registers of Scotland (RoS) data shows a total of 28,825 titles - 1.4% of the total - on the land register where the owner had an address outside the UK at the time of purchase.

Figures released to BBC Scotland shows that in the KY16 8 and KY16 9 postcodes in St Andrews, 5,494 of the titles in the land register were lodged with people or firms based in Scotland at the time of purchase - 81% of the total.

A further 845 (12%) were registered to addresses in the rest of the UK, and 444 (7%) were outside the UK.

A breakdown of the properties registered overseas shows they went to a total of 51 different countries or crown dependences, including Russia and the Cayman Islands.

A total of 164 St Andrews titles went to a United States address (37% of all overseas registrations), followed by Switzerland (30) and Hong Kong (28).

RoS data shows that St Andrews is ranked fourth out of the top ten postcode sectors in Scotland with the most overseas buyers.

Areas of Edinburgh make up the nine other top ten postcodes, with the top place being the Quartermile development, where more than a third of the properties in the development were bought by people based overseas .

Local estate agents have reported a steady trade in wealthy parents buying local homes for their children to live in during their time at university, as well as people attracted to the town by its golf courses.

Data from property firm Rettie shows the average sale price for houses in St Andrews over the last 12 months was £482,879 - more than twice the Scottish average - and up from £312,464 a decade ago.

Dr John Boyle, the firm's director of research and strategy, said the Fife town was a "hot market in a Scottish context".

He added: "When the tourists come here they think this might not be a bad place to retire to.

"So you've got a lot of downsizer demand within the community and you've got the university setting so both a lot of students and a lot of staff.

"St Andrews along with [Edinburgh's] New Town, Morningside and west end Glasgow, it's the handful of real prime areas across the country

"It's very sought after by a whole range of different buyers including buyers that have got significant amounts of money to go and spend on finding a place to live there."

Locals want 'sensible conversations' about the future

Ben Stuart, director of residential and business services at the University of St Andrews, highlighted its annual £480m contribution to Scotland's economy, supporting 9,000 jobs in the Fife and Tayside area.

He said: "St Andrews obviously borders with the ocean and green belts. There's not a lot of space left to provide that type of housing.

"All entities have to get together here and understand how they can relieve the pressures.

"Students are often unfairly blamed for the housing situation, when evidence shows it is a much more complex picture."

Stuart said this was reflected in property prices and the trends identified by BBC Scotland News.

He added: "Quite often, those with the deepest pockets are simply outbidding - by a substantial margin - locals who try to acquire property in town.

"And often those with the deepest pockets are from overseas."

Debbie MacCallum, a local entrepreneur and chairwoman of St Andrews Business Improvement District, said the town's international profile supported thousands of jobs and was "hugely valuable to our local businesses and the wider economy".

She added: "However, a globally recognised town also has to work for the people who live here all year-round and St Andrews is, first and foremost, a community.

"As demand for property grows, we need to continue having sensible conversations about how we balance the benefits of international investment with the need for homes, businesses and services that support a thriving local community."

The big looming change in the local housing market is new developments on the town's outskirts that will deliver more than 1,000 new homes.

This will increase the overall supply but John Mills, head of housing for Fife Council, also pointed out that 30% of the homes on these sites would be affordable housing.

He added: "We know that finding affordable housing in St Andrews is a major challenge and there is no single solution.

"That's why we're taking a range of steps to help improve housing options for local people."

Mills pointed to polices such as control areas for the number of short-term lets and an ongoing review of how key workers are allocated council housing.

articles.summary: Anonymous social media posts promoted a Charlie Kirk look-alike contest called "Kirkiversary" at the University of South Carolina ahead of the Sept. 10 anniversary of Kirk's killing.
articles.body: An apparent Charlie Kirk look-alike contest called "Kirkiversary" is being advertised at the University of South Carolina for Sept. 10, the anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination. Kirk, the 31-year-old founder of Turning Point USA, was assassinated Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University during his "American Comeback Tour." It was not immediately clear who created the post or organized the apparent event, whether those involved are USC students or not. ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR Libs of TikTok amplified the post Wednesday, characterizing the contest as an event organized by students to celebrate Kirk’s assassination and calling it "demonic." The University of South Carolina replied to the Libs of TikTok post saying, "We have no record of any registered student organization planning such an event. No university resources will be used to support this. DM us if you’d like a contact here that can help verify claims like this ahead of posting." articles.body: NEW DELHI: When the 'Flying Kremlin' and other ultra-secure aircraft touch down in Delhi this weekend, they won't just bring Russian President Vladimir Putin and other high-profile world leaders to the Brics Summit, they will land with a fully autonomous fortress-on-wheels featuring personal food-testing labs, decoy dignitaries and armoured limousines built to survive landmines and chemical attacks.As Delhi transforms into an impenetrable, multi-layered defensive grid, security personnel are bracing for a high-stakes security operation where AI-aimed snipers scan rooftops, gesture-recognition cameras spot human posture shifts, commandos slither down ropes from hovering helicopters and anti-graffiti strike teams patrol the streets 24/7, guarding against everything from high-tech threats to stealth protest tactics.The capital, sources said, hasn't seen security this tight since the 2023 G20 summit, and preparations this time are even more extensive. Unmanned aerial vehicles have been categorised as one of the most potent threats, and systems that can jam drone signals or shoot them down have been installed at several locations.Every dignitary or their hotel or carcade has been assigned a code name or call sign to ensure they are guided smoothly between locations without any overlap or security glitches. Intelligence inputs have hinted at the possibility of flash protests and spray-painting of inflammatory slogans near the venues, targeting some foreign leaders. Cops have formed anti-graffiti teams for round-the-clock patrolling to thwart any such attempts.President Putin's security grid comprises a sophisticated protective shield managed jointly by Russia's Federal Protective Service (FSO) and Indian counter-terrorism forces. Ground mobility will be centred around his custom-made, heavily armoured Aurus Senat limousine, often referred to as a "rolling bunker". Transported directly from Moscow, the state car is built to withstand chemical attacks, landmines and sniper fire, complete with run-flat tyres and an independent emergency oxygen supply.Up in the air, the Russian leader travels in a specially modified Ilyushin IL-96-300PU aircraft, known as the "Flying Kremlin", which operates alongside decoy jets, advanced missile-defence countermeasures and secure command systems. On the ground, the innermost protective layer comprises elite officers from Russian Presidential Security Service (SBP), supported by advanced FSO teams that sanitise every scheduled and potential itinerary venue. The Russian delegation manages its own strict logistics, travelling with personal chefs, portable testing laboratories for food and drink, and measures to collect biological waste, alongside deploying dummy dignitaries in select hotels to boost operational security.Securing the designated summit hotels in central Delhi, Aerocity and Gurgaon presented one of the most formidable logistical challenges for intelligence and law enforcement agencies. Every hotel is being managed as an independent secure zone under its assigned DCP venue commander, supervised by special commissioner-rank officers overseeing broader zones.Within each hotel, two rooms have been repurposed into operational command posts: a primary security control room linked directly to Delhi Police's central C4i command node and a secondary contingency room dedicated to emergency management.To prevent unauthorised access, advanced AI cameras equipped with posture-detection and intrusion-alert software monitor perimeter walls and hallways, capable of flagging unusual physical movements like crawling or wall-scaling. articles.title: Should you be 'cycle-syncing' your workouts?
articles.summary: Menstrual cycles are highly individual, making blanket advice found on social media difficult to apply, researchers say.
articles.body:
A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises.

"When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers.

This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'.

So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag.

Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts.

They divide the menstrual cycle into phases, recommending:

gradually increasing intensity in the follicular phase leading up to ovulation

harder strength or high-intensity training around ovulation

easing off again during the luteal phase (between ovulation and the start of your period)

Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle.

But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence".

"There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says.

A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next.

That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains.

Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception.

"It's not so much about doing certain exercises in certain phases, it's about working with your own individual body and what your needs might be."

Intuitive changes rather than strict plans

Cesci Burgoyne, a nurse based in Sydney, Australia who is also a qualified personal trainer and nutritionist, adjusts her training depending on how she feels in her cycle. She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively.

"In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC. "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier. I like to try and get my long runs in."

Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women.

Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month.

But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play".

Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating.

"The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable".

Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase.

"A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says.

She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs.

McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress. Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life.

Building strength requires consistent, progressively challenging training, she says, and "we don't want to create another barrier by suggesting women train less for almost half the month."

Dr Bate also warns against normalising severe symptoms: if pain, fatigue or mood changes interfere with exercise or daily life, women should seek medical advice rather than assuming it is an inevitable part of their cycle, she says.

While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware".

McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month.

Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules.

In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued.

For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel".

In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules.

articles.title: Trump makes 9/11 about himself, won't mark 25th anniversary at Ground Zero
articles.summary: US News: In President Donald Trump's telling at a White House event on Tuesday, two firefighters bodily lifted him to safety from a site near an unstable build.
articles.body: In President Donald Trump's telling at a White House event on Tuesday, two firefighters bodily lifted him to safety from a site near an unstable building after the Sept 11, 2001 attacks. "And I'll never forget," Trump said, "we thought it was coming down on top of us, and two firemen, big strong guys - and I'm not the smallest guy in the world - they grabbed me under the arm, said, 'Got to get out of here!'" Trump said.His comments, at an event honouring emergency personnel killed on 9/11, appeared to be a new instalment in a constantly evolving narrative that Trump has told over the years about his actions after the attacks. It's a story that has long featured the New York property tycoon as the hero, with variations on him taking workers down to Ground Zero.But Trump's version of events is one that US media say is disputed by rescue officials present at the time. The remarks also come amid a stir about Trump not being present as president in New York for the 25th anniversary of the attacks in which 2,977 people were killed. Instead of being at the site where Al-Qaeda hijackers rammed planes into the World Trade Center towers, Trump will pay his respects on Friday at the Pentagon in Washington, another target in the attacks.Trump and the White House have hotly denied reports that he chose the Pentagon because he was not allowed to deliver a speech at the 9/11 memorial. "This is more Corrupt News, I've been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks; it's a 'solemn ceremony!'" Trump said on his Truth Social network last week. Vice President JD Vance and Trump's living predecessors - Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, as well as Republican George Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks - are all expected at "Ground Zero." Later on Friday, Trump is due to fly to Ireland where he will attend the Irish Open golf tournament at his family's golf course over the weekend.His absence from New York marks a contrast with Trump's usual approach, which has been to put himself at the heart of the 9/11 story. Two days after the attacks, Trump told reporters that he had been to Ground Zero and had sent 100 workers to the site to help with recovery efforts. CNN and New York Times said people present at the site disputed his account.In the event on the White House Ellipse on Tuesday, where a steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center's South Tower was on display, Trump gave a fresh account of his actions that day. Trump said it had been a "beautiful morning" and that he had then seen a news alert on television, before looking out of his window "and I saw things that I never want to see again".Trump clarified his recollections in a lengthy Truth Social Post Tuesday evening. "I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers," Trump wrote, in a post accompanied by a video showing answering reporters' questions. "I was there as soon as the Law allowed," the US president added, as he lashed out at journalists and accused them of spreading "fake news".(This is an AFP story)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A dog refused to leave the house before a mini tornado hit a Cornish village on 23 Jan 2025; its owner says it saved his life
articles.summary: UK News: A dog's unusual refusal to leave the house may have saved its owner from walking directly into the path of a violent mini tornado that tore through a .
articles.body: A dog's unusual refusal to leave the house may have saved its owner from walking directly into the path of a violent mini tornado that tore through a Cornish village. Stephen Jeffrey had been preparing to take his cocker spaniel, Sevi, for a walk when the dog suddenly refused to go outside. Minutes later, powerful winds swept through Quintrell Downs near Newquay, uprooting trees, tearing away roof tiles and damaging homes. According to ITV News West Country, Jeffrey believes Sevi's strange and unprecedented behaviour kept them both out of danger.How a dog refusal to leave the house may have saved its owner's lifeThe incident happened on the morning of 23 January 2025 when Jeffrey was getting Sevi ready for their usual walk. The dog had his coat and lead on, and Jeffrey opened the front door expecting him to head outside. Instead, Sevi refused.According to ITV News West Country, the cocker spaniel had never behaved this way before. No matter what happened, the dog simply would not leave the house. Jeffrey eventually accepted his pet's decision and shut the door rather than forcing him outside. That ordinary decision soon took on an extraordinary meaning.A violent storm swept through the Cornish village of EnglandJeffrey had walked into the kitchen when the powerful winds struck Quintrell Downs shortly after that. The weather event moved through the area with such force that it caused widespread damage within a short period.ITV News West Country reported that trees were uprooted, roof tiles were torn away and walls were toppled as the mini tornado passed through the village. For residents caught nearby, the sudden violence of the winds was deeply frightening.Jeffrey later described the experience as horrifying. Looking back at the timing of Sevi's refusal, he believed that he and his dog would have been directly in the path of the storm had they gone outside as planned.For him, the dog's unexpected decision was not just unusual behaviour. He saw it as the moment that potentially saved his life.Did Sevi sense that something was wrongIt remains unclear why Sevi refused to go outside at that particular moment. ITV News West Country reported Jeffrey's belief that the dog seemingly sensed something was wrong, but there was no explanation offered for exactly what prompted the behaviour.Dogs can sometimes react differently to unfamiliar sounds or changes in their surroundings, but in this case, the most striking detail was that Jeffrey had never known Sevi to refuse a walk in this way before.Homes and gardens were left badly damaged by the tornadoThe storm's impact was felt across the village, with residents describing scenes of serious destruction. According to ITV News West Country, Rosemary Bray's home and garden had suffered extensive damage.She said her roof was gone, while her greenhouse, fencing and garden had also been badly affected. The sudden noise and force of the weather were so alarming that she initially thought something like an aircraft was crashing nearby and took shelter in her dining room.Her experience showed just how quickly the situation had changed for people in Quintrell Downs. What began as a normal morning turned into a frightening encounter with an intense burst of extreme weather. The damage was not limited to one property either.Sevi's decision became an unforgettable momentFor Stephen Jeffrey, the destruction around Quintrell Downs gave him a frightening sense of what might have happened if his usual morning walk had continued as planned. Instead, Sevi had stopped at the doorway.The dog could not explain why he refused to leave, and Jeffrey could not know what would have happened had they stepped outside. But after witnessing the force of the mini tornado, he was convinced that their decision to remain indoors had protected them from a dangerous situation.For residents of Quintrell Downs, the storm left damaged homes, broken structures and frightening memories. For Jeffrey, however, one moment stood apart from everything else when his normally willing cocker spaniel refused to take another step.What seemed like a strange decision at the time became, in his eyes, the reason he was still safe inside his home. And for Sevi, a walk that never happened may have become the most important one he ever refused.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iran war won't end until after US midterm elections, says Trump
articles.summary: The president also tells reporters he does not think oil prices will come down until after the crucial November vote.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.

"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Tehran on Wednesday.

His comments come as he headed to Texas for the party's first convention ahead of the midterms, when the balance of power could change in the US government.

Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war with Iran.

On Wednesday, oil prices rose to $100 (£74) for the first time since July due to increased fighting in the Middle East.

"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."

He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" - an apparent reference to the Democrats - "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".

Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons.

Trump says Iran war will end 'immediately after' midterms as he heads to Republican convention

Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".

The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings.

Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and any item that requires shipping.

On Wednesday, the US military said it had attacked five oil tanker ships with ties to Iran. Tehran, in response, launched attacks on two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels, according to Iranian state media.

A day earlier, the Iran-linked Houthis in Yemen launched a wave of attacks in Saudi Arabia, sparking fires at oil facilities.

The fighting, which began again recently after a 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, has also raised predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates in the US.

articles.title: Got a migraine, acne or ear infection? Go to your chemist first
articles.summary: Pharmacies in England will soon offer treatments for a total of 12 common conditions which save people going to their GP first.
articles.body:
People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first.

Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions - sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections.

Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list.

NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently.

After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen.

"For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said.

Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time".

The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are:

hay fever or allergic rhinitis in children

mild to moderate acne in young people and adults

Initially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says.

There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England.

Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations.

The charity the Migraine Trust said it was delighted by the news after calling for more help for migraine care in pharmacies.

Chief executive Rob Music said having this support for people with migraine through their local pharmacy was "a wonderful opportunity for a faster and improved care pathway".

Dr Amanda Doyle, director for primary care and community services at NHS England, said she wanted to make sure that patients can get as much support as possible in their communities, "so they do not have to be admitted to hospital unnecessarily".

But bodies representing pharmacies across England have consistently said that the funding provided by the goverment does not cover the workload for the new plans.

"Pharmacies are still under significant financial pressures," said Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association.

"This shows why the government should go much further and invest in our pharmacy network that has the power to transform people's experience of everyday health issues."

The Pharmacy First scheme started in England in 2024. NHS figures suggest it has delivered 14 million consultations since then, including two million appointments for sore throats and 1.7 million for urinary tract infections (UTIs).

People can be referred to their local pharmacy via NHS111 or by their GP, or just go direct to their high street chemist.

Scotland has a scheme which was seen as the model for England's Pharmacy First - Northern Ireland and Wales also have systems allowing pharmacies to treat patients with certain conditions.

Patients can be treated for 27 different conditions at chemists in Scotland.
